report:
**Conclusion:** No—not reliably. The best current evidence does **not** support a general claim that probiotics shorten acute infectious diarrhea.

A 2020 Cochrane review found probiotics probably make little or no difference in diarrhea persisting ≥48 hours, and that whether they reduce total duration remains uncertain. Earlier, smaller trials often suggested roughly a one-day benefit, but results were highly variable by probiotic strain, setting, and study quality; more recent, large, rigorous trials reduced confidence in that effect. [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33295643/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33295643/)

For example, a randomized placebo-controlled trial in 971 preschool children found that five days of *Lactobacillus rhamnosus* GG did not improve outcomes, including diarrhea duration. [https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1802598](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1802598)

Reflecting this evidence, the American Gastroenterological Association suggests **against** probiotics for children with acute infectious gastroenteritis. [https://gastro.org/clinical-guidance/role-of-probiotics-in-the-management-of-gastrointestinal-disorders/](https://gastro.org/clinical-guidance/role-of-probiotics-in-the-management-of-gastrointestinal-disorders/)

Probiotics are not interchangeable: effects, if any, are strain- and context-specific. Oral rehydration is the established priority; seek medical care for dehydration, bloody stool, high fever, severe pain, or persistent symptoms.
